facts.text: Copenhagen is one of the most bike-friendly cities in Europe; renting a bike is often faster and more pleasant than public transport for central-area sightseeing, but (as in Amsterdam) pedestrians need to stay out of marked bike lanes.

Copenhagen is one of the more expensive European capitals for food and drink - a casual lunch commonly runs 100-150 DKK (~€13-20) and a sit-down dinner with drinks for two can easily exceed 700-900 DKK (~€95-120).

Nyhavn's waterfront restaurants (the famously photogenic colorful-house strip) charge a substantial premium for the view - food quality doesn't reliably match the price, and better options are a short walk away.
Tivoli Gardens charges separate entry and per-ride tickets (or a combined multi-ride pass) - easy to underestimate the total cost if only budgeting for the entry fee.
Many smaller Danish shops and even some market stalls are card-only now - carrying cash "just in case" is less useful in Copenhagen than in many other European cities.
New Nordic cuisine and smørrebrød (open sandwiches) dominate the food scene; vegetarian options are widely available in central Copenhagen's modern restaurant scene.
